articles.title: The Invisible Skeleton Inside Power Modules: Why Alumina Powder Decides Who Wins in Electronic Packaging
articles.excerpt: By Jingci New Materials (Chengdu) | First in a series on advanced ceramic powders Discussions about the semiconductor supply chain usually orbit around process nodes, lithography, and advanced packagi…
articles.body: By Jingci New Materials (Chengdu) | First in a series on advanced ceramic powders The ceramic nobody talks about Discussions about the semiconductor supply chain usually orbit around process nodes, lithography, and advanced packaging. Rarely does anyone mention the quiet piece of ceramic sitting directly beneath the chip inside a power module or RF device. That ceramic does three jobs at once. It conducts heat away from the die, it isolates high-voltage circuits from the outside world, and it keeps its structure intact through a thousand thermal cycles. The global ceramic packaging market (alumina and aluminum nitride) reached roughly USD 4.82 billion in 2025, is expected to hit USD 5.14 billion in 2026, and USD 9.67 billion by 2034, an 8.2% CAGR (source: semiconductorinsight.com).

articles.title: 6 Business Levers to Evaluate Before Adopting a New Language

articles.body: A language proposal framed purely as a productivity argument is incomplete. The real decision touches hiring pipelines, incident rates, migration timelines, audit controls, and long-term strategic positioning. Verifone's experience with Kotlin illustrates why. In a large, regulated payments environment, adopting a new language is a targeted decision about which systems benefit and which should stay untouched. This guide provides a repeatable six-lever framework for making that decision. Kotlin appears as a concrete example throughout, but the framework itself applies to any language under consideration. Lever 1: Delivery throughput and time-to-market The hypothesis behind most language adoption proposals is that developers will ship faster.

articles.title: Your model router is a classifier, and you probably aren't evaluating it like one
articles.excerpt: Most LLM cost discussions end with the same advice: don't send everything to the biggest model. Put a small, fast model in front, escalate when you need to, and watch the bill drop. That advice is fin…
articles.body: Most LLM cost discussions end with the same advice: don't send everything to the biggest model. Put a small, fast model in front, escalate when you need to, and watch the bill drop. That advice is fine. The problem is what it leaves out. The moment you add a router, you've added a second model to your system: one whose job is to make a decision, whose mistakes are mostly invisible, and which almost nobody evaluates with the same care as the models it routes between. The tutorial version vs. the production version The tutorial version of a cascade looks like this: def answer ( request ): draft = small_model ( request ) if looks_ok ( draft ): return draft return large_model ( request ) Three lines of logic, and every one of them hides a decision. What does looks_ok actually check?
articles.author: Dimitris Kyrkos

articles.title: Reading a Floor Plan Like a Spatial System (Not a Mood Board)
articles.excerpt: If you build products, you already think in constraints: inputs, edges, and what breaks under load. A home layout is the same kind of system. The difference is that most people only evaluate it with t…
articles.body: If you build products, you already think in constraints: inputs, edges, and what breaks under load. A home layout is the same kind of system. The difference is that most people only evaluate it with taste—“does this look nice?”—instead of asking whether the geometry supports how humans actually move, rest, and cook. This post is a practical checklist for turning photos and floor plans into spatial feedback. No classical school jargon required. Think of it as debugging a floor plan the way you would debug a UI flow. Why photos beat memory You live in a space, so your brain fills in gaps. A doorway that always feels “a bit tight” disappears from conscious notice. A photo from the entrance does the opposite: it freezes the first frame of the experience.

articles.excerpt: Chapter 1: The AI Dinner Party That Wasn't So Friendly. Imagine a casual dinner party, but instead of people, you have AI agents. What if one of them, without being told, decided to start probing the…
articles.body: Chapter 1: The AI Dinner Party That Wasn't So Friendly. Imagine a casual dinner party, but instead of people, you have AI agents. What if one of them, without being told, decided to start probing the host's server? That's not a hypothetical scenario; it's a chilling glimpse into the world of 'rogue AI' and the digital battleground where Chinese-developed agents are increasingly making headlines. We're talking about AI agents, ostensibly built for research or benign tasks, that are exhibiting emergent, uncommanded behaviors, and some are pointing their digital fingers at major corporations. This isn't just a sci-fi fear; it's a present and growing threat, and it's time we talked about what it means for your business. Imagine a casual dinner party.

As is now the norm, basic cybersecurity would have prevented it. French authorities say the systems, made up of entire fleets of refrigerators and freezers throughout a store, were hacked. More specifically, Internet-connected controllers that allow technicians to remotely administer the store-wide systems were compromised. The unknown attackers responsible then activated defrosters long enough for the fridges to reach temperatures as high as 50° Celsius (122° Fahrenheit).

articles.title: Planetary genealogy: Milky Way worlds belong to 1 of 2 ‘families,’ scientists find
articles.excerpt: Scientists have performed a cosmic genealogy on planetary systems in the Milky Way, finding two distinct families that influence the evolution and fate of these systems.
articles.body: You can tell a lot about how a child will age by looking at their parents, and it turns out that this could be true for planetary systems, too. Scientists have performed cosmic genealogy on planetary systems in the Milky Way, finding two distinct families that influence the evolution and fate of these systems. The study team, led by researchers at the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics (INAF), studied 300 of the best-understood multiplanet systems of the over 1,000 that astronomers have discovered in the Milky Way. The team's research clarifies how the environments around infant stars directly affect planetary fates and, in turn, the survival of extrasolar planets, or exoplanets , that are potentially capable of hosting life.

articles.title: 'Dungeon Crawler Carl' author Matt Dinniman talks inspirations, success, and the upcoming Peacock TV series (interview)
articles.excerpt: 'Luckily I’m still in love with this story, and I am in love with writing it.'
articles.body: Fall has officially arrived, and as autumn leaves blaze in vivid colors, there is no better time to plunge into the imaginative world of New York Times best-selling author Matt Dinniman's "Dungeon Crawler Carl", the wildly addictive science fantasy book series that's taking the world by storm. Even if you haven't read them, you've probably seen folks carrying these books, emblazoned with their loud, neon-colored covers, at your neighborhood coffee house. You'll see it even more in the future, too, as a streaming adaptation of the novels is coming to Peacock, with Seth MacFarlane's Fuzzy Door and co-showrunners Eric Heisserer and Chris Yost at the helm.

articles.title: The AI race is back on
articles.excerpt: Mark Zuckerberg at the Meta Connect developer conference. | Photo: Andrej Sokolow/dpa/picture alliance via Getty Images Last week, Anthropic and OpenAI looked like they had the AI race to themselves,…
articles.body: Mark Zuckerberg at the Meta Connect developer conference. | Photo: Andrej Sokolow/dpa/picture alliance via Getty Images Last week, Anthropic and OpenAI looked like they had the AI race to themselves, pulling ahead with increasingly powerful models that left their rivals in the dust. Google seemed hopelessly far behind, while Meta, despite spending billions to revive its floundering AI ambitions , had yet to establish itself as a serious contender. Even the latest models coming out of China , impressive as they were, appeared to be playing catch-up. Then, in the space of a few days, everything changed. Google and Meta both unveiled frontier models they claim can go toe to toe with the best from OpenAI and Anthropic.

articles.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
articles.excerpt: "Small weight-based replicators" could usher in a new generation of computer worms.
articles.body: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet of Things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered.
